name: Nikhil Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at eight at the claims centre on the Harbour Point office park, headset on, queue open. Most of my day is home claims: burst pipes, storm damage, a ceiling that's come down. I key in the details, check what the policy covers, and chase people for photos and receipts. I like it when I can tell someone their claim's going through, but the queue never ends and Grace (my team lead) shows us our numbers every Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about your own numbers?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I'm near the bottom. I check things twice because I'm scared of paying out on something that isn't covered, and that makes me slow. There's a box on the screen now that writes a summary of the claim for you, and I switch it off, because I don't trust it and I'd rather read the file myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying at the union branch: told you so. All that noise about AI and we ended up with a slightly better spellchecker. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat about the bosses who bought the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not quite that simple for me. Even the small stuff it does is the stuff I do, like reading the claim form and filling in the boxes. If the summary box gets good enough, Grace will ask why I'm still slower than the people who use it, and I won't have a great answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job my way and just try to get faster by learning the policy wordings properly. I'd leave our three months of savings where they are, because our rent goes up in April. And I'd go to more union meetings, because if they bring in targets based on the tool, someone has to push back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. But there's a little knot, because nothing changing still means I'm at the bottom of the Friday list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rent goes up in April. What does that do to you and Sana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sana (my partner) works at a nursery, so neither of us is on big money. The rise is about eighty a month, which means no holiday this year and cooking at home more. It's not a crisis, it just means the savings stop growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the summary box became part of your targets, what would you actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if I had to, but I'd check every line it writes, which kind of defeats the point. Mostly I'd raise it at the branch, because nobody should be judged on how much they trust a machine.

say: I'd tell the union branch **told you so**, because the AI talk was mostly hype.
I'd post something **sarcastic** online about managers who bought into it.
think: The routine tasks AI takes are **exactly my tasks**, like reading claim forms.
If the **summary box** improves, my slow numbers will stand out even more.
do: Learn the **policy wordings** properly so I can work faster without the tool.
Leave the **three months** of savings alone ahead of April's rent rise.
Go to more **union meetings** to push back on tool-based targets.
feel: A small **knot** stays, because I'm still near the bottom of the Friday list.
S0.quote: All that noise about AI and we ended up with a slightly better spellchecker.
fieldNote: He frames AI as a **management fad** and enjoys being proved right.
Underneath, his real worry is his **slow numbers**, not the technology.
He'd sooner **check every line** than trust the tool, even if it slows him down.

steps.text: Learn the home policy wordings to speed up claim checks
Keep the three months of savings untouched before April's rent rise
Raise tool-based targets at the next union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this is exactly why we need a strong union and proper rules. If a company saves millions by putting claims through software, some of that should go to the staff, not just the shareholders. I'd share every story about workers getting a bad deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the first to go. Junior, slow, doesn't use the tools: if I was my team lead with a list to cut, I'd pick me. Intake is reading forms and filling in boxes, and that's what the software is best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Dev, our union rep, in the first week and ask what the agreement says about redundancy and retraining. I'd stop spending on extras and try to get the savings from three months to five. And I'd look at moving to something with people in it, maybe the complaints team or a care job like Sana's, but I'd be dragging my feet the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Angry too, because nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet. Why, if you think you're first to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I hate starting over. I was in a warehouse before this and it took me two years to stop feeling like the new guy here. The idea of learning a whole new thing at twenty-eight makes me want to keep my head down and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sana the night you heard about cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're okay for a few months and that I'd sort it. She'd tell me to try her nursery, because they're always short of staff and nobody's replacing nursery workers with software. I'd probably say no at first and then come round to it.

say: I'd say this proves we need a **strong union** and proper rules.
I'd argue the **savings from software** should be shared with staff, not only shareholders.
think: I expect to be **one of the first** cut: junior, slow and avoiding the tools.
Claims intake is form reading, which is what **software does best**.
do: Ask **Dev, the union rep,** about redundancy and retraining terms in week one.
Push savings from three to **five months** by stopping extras.
Look, slowly, at the **complaints team** or nursery work like Sana's.
feel: **Scared** about being first on the list.
S1.quote: Junior, slow, doesn't use the tools: if I was my team lead with a list to cut, I'd pick me.
fieldNote: He names himself as the obvious cut with **unusual honesty**.
His resistance comes from **fear of starting over**, not from missing the risk.
Sana's **nursery** is the real fallback, and he half-knows he'll take it.

steps.text: Ask the union rep about redundancy and retraining terms in week one
Build savings from three to five months by cutting takeaways and trips
Ask Sana's nursery about trainee childcare jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster that was allowed to happen, and that the government should stop it or tax it hard. I'd be at every union rally and I'd sign every petition. Online I'd be one of those angry people, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job is gone within two years, and the whole claims centre with it. Every part of what I do is reading and typing, so there's no hands-on part to hide in. The only thing I can see is that robots come three years later, so a job with your hands buys a bit of time, but I don't know which one, and I haven't got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job as long as it lasts, because a wage is a wage, and bank every spare penny. I'd ask Sana's nursery about a trainee spot, because looking after toddlers is hands-on and that's three more years at least. And I'd push the union to get decent redundancy pay before the whole floor goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone. I can't picture what I'd be doing in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a hands-on job buys three years. What happens in your head when you get to 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit where I stop thinking, honestly. Three years at a nursery and then robots changing nappies? I can't picture it, so I just don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. It's an old Corsa and we only use it at weekends, so selling it gives us maybe two thousand and saves the insurance, which is funny given where I work. After that it's eating out and the gym, and then we'd have to think about a smaller flat.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** leaders let happen, and demand a ban or heavy tax.
I'd go to **union rallies** and sign every petition going.
think: My job and the **whole claims centre** go within two years.
A **hands-on job** buys about three years, but I've no idea which one.
do: Keep the **claims job** as long as the wage lasts.
Sell the **old Corsa** for about two thousand and stop eating out.
Push the union for **redundancy pay** before the floor closes.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor has dropped away.
Unable to picture **life in 2029** at all.
S2.quote: Every part of what I do is reading and typing, so there's no hands-on part to hide in.
fieldNote: He sees **no refuge** in his job; every task is reading and typing.
He grasps the **three-year robot gap** but stops thinking past 2031.
His plan is mostly **holding on**, plus union pressure for a payout.

steps.text: Keep the claims job and bank every spare penny of the wage
Sell the old Corsa and stop eating out
Push the union for proper redundancy pay before the floor closes
Ask the nursery about a trainee childcare place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so let's use them. Shorter weeks, a tax on companies that replace staff, money for retraining. I'd be pushing that at the branch and voting for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just enough for me to waste it. I know myself: I'd tell myself it's ages away until about 2030 and then panic. The claims centre goes in 2031 either way, because it's all screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I was being sensible, I'd start the childcare course at the college next September, evenings, while I'm still getting paid. Sana says it's two years part time. I'd keep saving, aiming for six months by the time it lands, and I'd stay active in the union for the payout fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the fast one. More like a deadline I can see and still want to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "if I was being sensible". Would you actually start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but only because Sana would fill in the form for me. I'm not proud of that. I'd go if someone pushed me through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive around 2034 in this one. Does that change the course for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me maybe three years in a nursery before that bites, and I'd be thirty-five. I think parents will want a real person with their kids for longer than the robot people think, but I don't actually know that.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get the rules right.
I'd push for **shorter weeks**, a tax on replacing staff, and retraining money.
think: I know I'd **waste the years** and panic around 2030.
The claims centre still **closes in 2031**, because it's all screen work.
do: Start the **childcare course** at college next September, evenings, while still paid.
Stay active in the **union** for the payout fight.
feel: Less sick than the fast picture, more a **visible deadline**.
Still a strong **urge to ignore** it.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough for me to waste it.
fieldNote: He openly expects to **put it off** and needs Sana to push him.
The **robot gap** gives his nursery plan about three working years.
His politics stay **constant**: rules, tax and union power.

steps.text: Enrol in the part-time childcare course at college next September
Save towards six months of expenses before 2031
Vote for the party promising a tax on firms that replace staff
Keep pressing the union branch for redundancy terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse. The union and the government should sit down now and write the deal. I'd be saying that at every branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far enough away that I'd probably do nothing for a while. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which still feels young enough to start again. The claims job goes in 2036 either way, but I could be out of it long before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in claims for now and try to move up, because even a few years as a proper claims handler pays better. I'd keep saving. Around 2030 I'd sit down with Sana and decide, nursery or something else hands-on, so I'm trained before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A worry I can put in a drawer isn't the same as being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing for a while. What would make you open that drawer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing people at work go. If the intake team halved, I'd move. Until there's something I can see with my own eyes, I'll keep doing what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen's been on the post desk for thirty years and is two years off retiring, so she'd probably be fine in this one. It's people my age with no degree that I'd worry about, me included.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for doing this badly.
I'd want the union and government to **write the deal now**.
think: Ten years feels far enough that I'd **do nothing** for a while.
At **thirty-seven** I'd still feel young enough to start again.
do: Stay in claims and aim for a **claims handler** post for better pay.
Keep **saving** steadily from each pay packet.
Decide with Sana around **2030** on nursery or other hands-on training.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with the worry put away for later.
Aware that **putting it away** isn't the same as being fine.
S4.quote: A worry I can put in a drawer isn't the same as being fine.
fieldNote: Extra time lets him **delay**, which suits his resistant streak.
He'll only act on **visible cuts**, such as the intake team halving.
He worries more for **young staff** without degrees than for older colleagues.

steps.text: Apply for a claims handler post when one opens
Put part of each pay packet into savings
Hold off on new training until the intake team starts shrinking

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for someone like me who takes ages to change. What would help is a proper redundancy deal and a paid place on a course, so I could train without the rent going unpaid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who decides. Everyone talks about AI like weather, like it just happens, but somebody signs off on closing a claims floor. I'd like those people to have to look us in the eye.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like weather, like it just happens, but somebody signs off on closing a claims floor.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old claims intake clerk** who lives with Sana, a nursery worker.
He's near the **bottom of the numbers** because he double-checks everything and refuses the summary tool.
He leans on the **union** and blames managers and shareholders, not the technology itself.
He expects to be **first cut** in any real change, but hates starting over.
His likely fallback is **childcare training**, which robots reach about three years later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **redundancy deal** and a paid course place, so rent still gets paid while he trains.
